title: Services
content:
We work with teams that have outgrown hand-run systems but do not want a vendor to own them. Engagements are scoped around a specific system or product, and end with your team able to build, deploy, and operate what we left behind.
Build Application development. Working software, not prototypes: a real implementation, tests that can fail, and a pipeline that ships it. In C, C++, Go, Python, and TypeScript, with performance measured before it is guessed at.
Event-driven systems. Systems that do their work in the background and at scale, so one slow dependency does not take the whole product down with it. Under the hood: partitioning and ordering, idempotent consumers, the transactional outbox, replay and recovery, and the backpressure that appears the moment a consumer slows. Most of the hard problems here are correctness problems wearing a throughput costume.
Delivery pipelines. Teams ship faster, and the safe path becomes the fast one so nobody is tempted to skip it under deadline. Build, test, sign, scan, and promote, in GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, or whatever you already run. This is where most engagements start.
Supply chain security. Nobody can ship compromised code into your production, and you can prove where any given deployment came from. Artefacts signed with Sigstore or cosign, SBOMs per build, verification enforced at admission, and provenance tracing a deployment back to the commit that produced it.
Run Platform and infrastructure as code. Your infrastructure described in version control and produced by a command, so it can be reviewed, rebuilt, and understood by someone who did not build it. Terraform modules and state hygiene, Ansible roles, and image pipelines. Delivered as a reviewed repository, not a hand-edited environment.
Kubernetes and GitOps. Production converges to what is in the repository, automatically, instead of drifting from it. Clusters built and hardened, workloads packaged as Helm charts and Kustomize overlays, and Argo CD doing the reconciling.
Cloud-agnostic architecture. Your systems do not break because a vendor changed its prices, retired a product, or had a bad week in one region. Multi-cloud and hybrid designs that keep the portable parts portable and pin the rest deliberately. OpenStack and on-premises included, because much of real infrastructure is neither AWS nor Kubernetes.
Configuration at scale. Configuration generated the same way code is, so it cannot silently drift from what you think is running. Deterministic builds, drift detection, and secrets handled through Vault rather than scattered across environment files.
Improve Observability and data. You know when something is wrong before your customers tell you, and the bill does not surprise you next quarter. The Grafana LGTM stack, open source and vendor-neutral: Prometheus, Loki, Tempo, and Mimir, deployed single-tenant or highly available and provisioned as code, wired to service level objectives rather than to a wall of panels. We design signal cost up front, because ingestion and retention are where observability budgets go. The data work sits on the same foundation: natural-language querying of your own telemetry, anomaly detection with a measured false-positive rate, capacity forecasting before the node runs out, cardinality analysis for the bill that grew without anyone deciding it should, classical modelling where a model is genuinely the right answer, and the data infrastructure under an existing analytics team.
Performance and reliability. The unglamorous work of making things smaller, faster, and harder to break. Profiling, capacity planning, load testing, and incident review that ends in a change rather than a document.
Legacy and long-lived systems. The system nobody wants to replace, and the engagement nobody wants to admit they signed. We work inside it rather than around it, under constraints you did not choose, and we are direct about what is worth keeping and what is not.
AI-assisted delivery, opt-in. Test generation, first-pass review, and pipeline debugging. The pipeline works identically without it, nothing reaches production unreviewed, and if it does not measurably beat your current process on your workload, we do not put it in. Most clients start with pipeline debugging and stop there.
